pool.q: Cengel Example 11–2. R-134a enters the compressor as superheated vapor at 0.14 MPa and −10 °C (h₁ = 246.36 kJ/kg) and leaves at 0.8 MPa and 50 °C (h₂ = 286.69 kJ/kg); the enthalpy after isentropic compression to 0.8 MPa would be h₂ₛ = 284.21 kJ/kg. The isentropic efficiency of the compressor is:
pool.e: η_c ≅ (h₂ₛ − h₁)/(h₂ − h₁) = (284.21 − 246.36)/(286.69 − 246.36) = 0.938 (printed 0.939). The inverse ratio gives 1.066 (> 1, impossible); h₂ₛ/h₂ forgets to subtract h₁.
pool.s: Cengel Example 11–2

pool.q: Cengel Example 11–2 (continued): the refrigerant leaves the condenser at 26 °C and 0.72 MPa (h₃ ≅ h_f@26 °C = 87.83 kJ/kg) and is throttled to 0.15 MPa; flow rate 0.05 kg/s. The COP of the refrigerator is:
pool.e: Q̇_L = 0.05·(246.36 − 87.83) = 7.93 kW; Ẇ_in = 0.05·(286.69 − 246.36) = 2.02 kW; COP = 3.93 (printed 3.93: below the 3.97 of the ideal cycle because compression is not isentropic, despite the subcooling). 3.74 uses h₃ of the ideal cycle; 4.19 uses the isentropic work.
pool.s: Cengel Example 11–2

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–18: R-134a enters the compressor at 0.14 MPa, −10 °C, 0.12 kg/s and leaves at 0.7 MPa, 50 °C; it leaves the condenser at 24 °C (h₃ ≅ 84.98 kJ/kg). The rate of heat removal from the refrigerated space (kW) is:
pool.e: Q̇_L = ṁ(h₁ − h₄) = 0.12·(246.36 − 84.98) = 19.4 kW (printed 19.4 kW). Using h₃ = 95.47 (saturated liquid at 0.8 MPa from another problem) gives 18.1; 24.4 is Q̇_H.
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–18

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–18 (b): h₁ = 246.36 kJ/kg (0.14 MPa, −10 °C), h₂ = 288.53 kJ/kg (0.7 MPa, 50 °C); h₂ₛ is taken at 0.7 MPa with s = s₁ = 0.9724 kJ/(kg·K). The isentropic efficiency of the compressor is about:
pool.e: η_c = (h₂ₛ − h₁)/(h₂ − h₁) = (281.2 − 246.36)/(288.53 − 246.36) = 82.6 % by table interpolation ≈ 82.5 % (printed 82.5 %; CoolProp 82.5 %). The inverse ratio gives 121.0 % (> 100 %, impossible); h₂ₛ/h₂ forgets to subtract h₁; 1 − η_c is the loss fraction.
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–18

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–22: R-134a enters the evaporator at 120 kPa with quality 0.3; ideal cycle, the condenser leaves saturated liquid. The enthalpy h₄ = h₃ of the refrigerant (kJ/kg) is:
pool.e: h₄ = h_f + x·h_fg = 22.49 + 0.3·214.48 = 86.8 kJ/kg; throttling keeps the enthalpy so h₃ = h₄. 22.5 is x = 0; h_g − 0.3h_fg corresponds to x = 0.7; 0.3h_g drops h_f.
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–22

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–32: an R-134a heat pump heats a house losing 60,000 kJ/h; the refrigerant enters the compressor at 280 kPa, 0 °C (h₁ = 250.83 kJ/kg), leaves at 1 MPa, 60 °C (h₂ = 293.38) and leaves the condenser at 30 °C (h₃ = 93.58). The electric power of the heat pump (kW) is:
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–32

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–2: reversed Carnot cycle with R-134a, condensing at 30 °C (saturated vapor → saturated liquid), evaporator pressure 160 kPa (T_sat = −15.60 °C). The COP is:
pool.e: T_L = 257.55 K, T_H = 303.15 K ⇒ COP_R = 1/(T_H/T_L − 1) = 5.648 ≈ 5.64 (printed 5.64; the book uses 273 K, giving 5.645). COP_HP = COP_R + 1 = 6.65 belongs to a heat pump; T_L/T_H = 0.85 is not yet the COP; using °C instead of K gives nonsense.
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–2

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–97: open gas refrigeration cycle on an aircraft: air at 30 °C, 100 kPa is compressed isentropically to 250 kPa, cooled to 70 °C, then expanded isentropically through the turbine to 100 kPa. The temperature of the air entering the cabin (°C) is about:
pool.e: T₄ = T₃/r_p^((k−1)/k) = 343.15/2.5^0.2857 = 264.1 K = −9.0 °C (printed −9 °C). Using °C in the formula gives 23 or 54; dividing T by r_p (no exponent) gives −136.
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–97 (§11-8)

pool.q: Cengel Example 11–5 (English units, Table A-17E). An ideal gas refrigeration cycle using air keeps a space at 0 °F (460 R, compressor inlet) and rejects heat to the surroundings at 80 °F (540 R, turbine inlet); the pressure ratio of the compressor is 4. With variable specific heats, the COP of the cycle is:
pool.e: A-17E: h₁ = 109.90 Btu/lbm, P_r1 = 0.7913 ⇒ P_r2 = 4P_r1 ⇒ T₂ = 683 R, h₂ = 163.5; h₃ = 129.06, P_r3 = 1.3860 ⇒ P_r4 = P_r3/4 ⇒ T₄ = 363 R, h₄ = 86.7. q_L = 23.2; w_net = 53.6 − 42.39 ⇒ COP = 2.071 ≈ 2.06 (printed 2.06; w_net is a difference of large numbers, so a 0.05 Btu/lbm rounding moves the COP by 1 %). The constant-k formula, 1/(4^0.2857 − 1) = 2.06, almost coincides over this narrow temperature range; inverting the ratio gives 0.48; q_L/w_comp ignores the turbine work and gives 0.43; (h₂ − h₃)/w_net = 3.07 is the heat-pump COP.
pool.s: Cengel Example 11–5 (§11-8)

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–110 (FE). Consider a heat pump that operates on the reversed Carnot cycle with R-134a as the working fluid executed under the saturation dome between the pressure limits of 140 and 800 kPa. R-134a changes from saturated vapor to saturated liquid during the heat rejection process. The net work input for this cycle is
pool.e: T_L = T_sat@140 kPa = −18.77 °C, T_H = T_sat@800 kPa = 31.31 °C. In the Carnot cycle under the dome s₃ − s₄ = s_fg@800 kPa = 0.5643 kJ/(kg·K), so w_net = (T_H − T_L)·s_fg = (31.31 − (−18.77))·0.5643 = 28.3 kJ/kg. 144 kJ/kg is the heat absorbed q_L; 275 kJ/kg is h₂ of the vapor-compression cycle, not the Carnot work.
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–110 (FE)

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–111 (FE). A refrigerator removes heat from a refrigerated space at −5°C at a rate of 0.35 kJ/s and rejects it to an environment at 20°C. The minimum required power input is
pool.e: The minimum power corresponds to a Carnot refrigerator: COP = T_L/(T_H − T_L) = 268.15/25 = 10.73; Ẇ = Q̇_L/COP = 350 W/10.73 = 32.6 W ≈ 33 W. 350 W is Q̇_L itself; 30 W is what you get if 0.35 kJ/s were taken as Q̇_H of a Carnot heat pump (Ẇ = Q̇_H(1 − T_L/T_H) = 29.8 W).
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–111 (FE)

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–112 (FE). A refrigerator operates on the ideal vapor compression refrigeration cycle with R-134a as the working fluid between the pressure limits of 120 and 800 kPa. If the rate of heat removal from the refrigerated space is 32 kJ/s, the mass flow rate of the refrigerant is
pool.e: h₁ = h_g@120 kPa = 236.97, h₃ = h₄ = h_f@800 kPa = 95.47 kJ/kg ⇒ q_L = 141.50 kJ/kg; ṁ = Q̇_L/q_L = 32/141.50 = 0.226 kg/s ≈ 0.23. 0.81 kg/s divides 32 kW by the specific compressor work (39.4 kJ/kg); 0.15 kg/s divides by h_fg@120 kPa (214.5 kJ/kg).
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–112 (FE)

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–113 (FE). A heat pump operates on the ideal vapor compression refrigeration cycle with R-134a as the working fluid between the pressure limits of 0.32 and 1.2 MPa. If the mass flow rate of the refrigerant is 0.193 kg/s, the rate of heat supply by the heat pump to the heated space is
pool.e: h₁ = h_g@0.32 MPa = 251.88; s₁ = 0.9301; h₂ (1.2 MPa, s₁) = 279.37; h₃ = h_f@1.2 MPa = 117.77 kJ/kg. Q̇_H = ṁ(h₂ − h₃) = 0.193·(279.37 − 117.77) = 31.2 kW ≈ 31. 26 kW is Q̇_L (= ṁ(h₁ − h₄) = 25.9); the compressor power is only 5.3 kW.
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–113 (FE)

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–114 (FE). An ideal vapor compression refrigeration cycle with R-134a as the working fluid operates between the pressure limits of 120 kPa and 1000 kPa. The mass fraction of the refrigerant that is in the liquid phase at the inlet of the evaporator is
pool.e: h₄ = h₃ = h_f@1000 kPa = 107.32 kJ/kg; at 120 kPa: h_f = 22.49, h_fg = 214.48 ⇒ x₄ = (107.32 − 22.49)/214.48 = 0.396 (vapor). The liquid fraction = 1 − x₄ = 0.604 ≈ 0.60. 0.40 is the VAPOR fraction (x₄), not the liquid fraction.
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–114 (FE)

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–115 (FE). Consider a heat pump that operates on the ideal vapor compression refrigeration cycle with R-134a as the working fluid between the pressure limits of 0.32 and 1.2 MPa. The coefficient of performance of this heat pump is
pool.e: COP_HP = q_H/w = (h₂ − h₃)/(h₂ − h₁) = 161.60/27.49 = 5.88 ≈ 5.9 (= COP_R + 1 with COP_R = 4.88). 4.9 is the COP_R of the refrigerator on the same cycle.
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–115 (FE)

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–116 (FE). An ideal gas refrigeration cycle using air as the working fluid operates between the pressure limits of 80 and 280 kPa. Air is cooled to 35°C before entering the turbine. The lowest temperature of this cycle is
pool.e: The lowest temperature is T₄ (turbine exit): T₄ = T₃/r_p^((k−1)/k) = 308.15/(280/80)^0.2857 = 308.15/1.4304 = 215.4 K = −57.7 °C ≈ −58 °C. Using °C in the formula gives 35/1.4308 ≈ 24 °C (answer e).
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–116 (FE)

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–117 (FE). Consider an ideal gas refrigeration cycle using helium as the working fluid. Helium enters the compressor at 100 kPa and −10°C and compressed to 250 kPa. Helium is then cooled to 20°C before it enters the turbine. For a mass flow rate of 0.2 kg/s, the net power input required is
pool.e: He (A-2a): c_p = 5.1926 kJ/(kg·K), k = 1.667 ⇒ (k − 1)/k = 0.4001; 2.5^0.4003 = 1.4429. T₁ = 263.15 K ⇒ T₂ = 379.7 K; T₃ = 293.15 K ⇒ T₄ = 203.2 K. w_net = c_p[(T₂ − T₁) − (T₃ − T₄)] = 5.1926·[116.5 − 90.0] = 137.92 kJ/kg; Ẇ = 0.2·137.92 = 27.6 kW. 93.5 kW is the turbine work alone (93.4 kW), not the net work; the compressor work alone is 121.0 kW.
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–117 (FE)

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–119 (FE). Consider a refrigerator that operates on the vapor compression refrigeration cycle with R-134a as the working fluid. The refrigerant enters the compressor as saturated vapor at 160 kPa, and exits at 800 kPa and 50°C, and leaves the condenser as saturated liquid at 800 kPa. The coefficient of performance of this refrigerator is
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–119 (FE)

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–84. A thermoelectric refrigerator removes heat from a refrigerated space at −5°C at a rate of 130 W and rejects it to an environment at 20°C. The maximum coefficient of performance this thermoelectric refrigerator can have is:
pool.e: The maximum COP is that of a Carnot machine between the two temperatures (same temperature limits, whether thermoelectric or vapor-compression): COP = T_L/(T_H − T_L) = 268.15/25 = 10.73 (printed 10.72 because the book uses 273 K; minimum power 130/10.72 = 12.1 W, printed 12.1 W). 11.73 puts T_H in the numerator (the Carnot heat-pump COP); 11.73 adds 1.
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–84

pool.q: Which statement correctly defines "refrigeration"?
o: Transfer of heat from a lower-temperature region to a higher-temperature one
Transfer of heat from a higher-temperature region to a lower-temperature one
Lowering the pressure of the fluid by a throttling valve
Converting all the heat received into mechanical work
pool.e: Slide p.3: refrigeration is the transfer of heat from a lower-temperature region to a higher-temperature one: against the natural direction, so work is needed (a refrigeration cycle). The natural direction (high → low) needs no machine; turning all heat into work violates the second law; throttling is only one step of the cycle.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.3: Refrigerators, heat pumps, COP

pool.q: The most frequently used refrigeration cycle is:
o: the Otto cycle of gasoline engines
the Rankine steam cycle of power plants
pool.e: Slide p.3: the vapor-compression cycle, in which the refrigerant is vaporized and condensed alternately and compressed in the vapor phase. The reversed Carnot cycle is only a standard of comparison (p.14); Otto is a power cycle.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.3: Refrigerators, heat pumps, COP

pool.q: For fixed Q_L and Q_H, how is the COP of a heat pump related to the COP of a refrigerator?
o: COP_HP = COP_R (the two coefficients are equal)
COP_HP = COP_R − 1 (so it can be below 1)
pool.e: Q_H = Q_L + W ⇒ COP_HP = Q_H/W = (Q_L + W)/W = COP_R + 1 (Cengel Eq. 11–3). Because COP_R > 0, COP_HP > 1: a heat pump is at worst a resistance heater. Slide p.9 only introduces the two machines; the relation is added from the book.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.9 + Cengel §11-1 (added from the book)

pool.q: In the slide's table of phase transitions, which pair of processes both ABSORB heat from the surroundings?
pool.e: The table on slide p.6: melting (solid → liquid), evaporation (liquid → gas) and sublimation (solid → gas) absorb heat; freezing, condensation and desublimation (gas → solid) emit heat. The vapor-compression cycle uses exactly this: evaporation in the evaporator (absorbs Q_L), condensation in the condenser (releases Q_H).
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.6: Latent heat, phase change

pool.q: At atmospheric pressure, compare the heat to evaporate 1 kg of liquid water at 100 °C with the heat to warm 1 kg of liquid water from 0 °C to 100 °C (steam Table A-4). The heat of vaporization is larger by about:
pool.e: Table A-4: h_fg@100 °C = 2,256.4 kJ/kg; warming from 0 °C (h_f ≈ 0) to 100 °C: h_f(100 °C) − h_f(0.01 °C) = 419.2 kJ/kg. Ratio = 2,256.4/419.2 = 5.4. The plot on p.7 is a sketch not to scale (the horizontal segment looks shorter than the heating segment): in reality the evaporation segment is about 5 times longer.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.7 + Table A-4

pool.q: On the slide's log p–h diagram, what does the line x = 0.4 in the wet-vapour region mean?
o: All states in which 40 % of the mass is vapor and 60 % is liquid
All states in which 40 % of the mass is liquid and 60 % is vapor
All states at 0.4 of the critical temperature
All states at 0.4 of the critical pressure
pool.e: x is the quality (vapour content): the mass fraction of vapor in the mixture. x = 0 is the boiling line (saturated liquid), x = 1 the saturated-vapour line. Slide p.8 marks x = 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.8: Wet region and log p–h

pool.q: In the wet-vapour region of the log p–h diagram (slide p.8), how does an isotherm (T = 273 K or 293 K) run?
o: Vertically, because enthalpy stays constant when the temperature is constant throughout the wet region
Coincident with the quality line x = 0.5, curving down toward the right of the diagram
Sloping upward to the right, because the temperature rises gradually as the quality x rises in the wet region
Horizontally, because the phase change occurs at constant pressure when the temperature is constant
pool.e: In the wet region T and p are tied together (saturation pressure): constant T means constant p, so isotherms are horizontal (the horizontal red/blue segments on p.8). In the liquid region isotherms are nearly vertical, in the vapour region they curve downward.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.8: Wet region and log p–h

pool.q: When the Carnot cycle is reversed, what happens to the directions of heat and work, and which way does the cycle run on the T–s diagram?
o: All heat and work interactions reverse; the cycle runs counterclockwise on T–s
Only the heat reverses while the work keeps its direction; the cycle runs counterclockwise
Nothing reverses; only the state labels change, so the cycle still absorbs heat at T_H
Only the work reverses while the heat flows keep their directions; the cycle still runs clockwise
pool.e: Slide p.11: reversing the Carnot cycle also reverses every heat and work interaction. Heat is taken at T_L, rejected at T_H, and work must be supplied. On T–s the cycle runs counterclockwise (Cengel §11-2, added).
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.11 + Cengel §11-2 (added from the book)

pool.q: In the slide's reversed Carnot cycle, which process is the isentropic compression and which is the isothermal heat rejection?
o: Isentropic compression is 1→2; isothermal heat rejection is 3→4
Isentropic compression is 2→3; isothermal heat rejection is 3→4
Isentropic compression is 3→4; isothermal heat rejection is 1→2
Isentropic compression is 4→1; isothermal heat rejection is 2→3
pool.e: Slide p.12: 1→2 isothermal absorption of Q_L at T_L; 2→3 isentropic compression (temperature rises to T_H); 3→4 isothermal rejection of Q_H at T_H (saturated vapor → saturated liquid); 4→1 isentropic expansion (temperature drops to T_L).
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.12: Reversed Carnot cycle

pool.q: According to the slide's formula COP_R,Carnot = 1/(T_H/T_L − 1), when does the COP of a Carnot refrigerator increase?
o: When T_L falls or T_H rises (the two temperatures move apart)
Never: the Carnot COP is a constant of the fluid
When T_L rises or T_H falls (temperatures come closer)
Only when T_H rises, whatever T_L is
pool.e: The smaller T_H/T_L (the closer the two temperatures), the smaller the denominator T_H/T_L − 1 and the larger the COP. Example: T_L = 263.15 K, T_H = 313.15 K: COP = 5.26; with T_L = 273.15 K the COP = 6.83. The Carnot COP depends only on the two temperatures, not on the fluid.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.13: Reversed Carnot cycle

pool.q: According to the slide, what is the role of the reversed Carnot cycle in refrigeration?
o: The cycle that most refrigerators and air conditioners actually use in practice because it has the highest COP
The cycle with the lowest COP between two specified temperature levels, used as the worst case
A standard against which real refrigeration cycles are compared; not practical in reality
A cycle used only for heat pumps, never for refrigerators, because it needs a turbine
pool.e: Slide p.14: the reversed Carnot cycle is the most efficient refrigeration cycle between two given temperature levels (largest COP), an ideal but impractical cycle, and a standard for comparison. Cengel §11-2 gives the reason: 2→3 compresses a liquid–vapor mixture and 4→1 expands a high-moisture fluid in a turbine, both hard to realise (added).
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.14: Reversed Carnot cycle

pool.q: Which two changes does the ideal vapor-compression cycle make to remove the impracticalities of the reversed Carnot cycle?
o: Vaporize the refrigerant completely before compression; replace the turbine with a throttling valve
Use a gas instead of a vapor, replace the evaporator by a regenerator and keep the turbine
Cool the refrigerant to compressed liquid before the compressor; replace the throttling valve with a turbine
Compress isothermally instead of isentropically, and remove the condenser by cooling in the evaporator
pool.e: Slide p.15: vaporize completely before compression (the compressor only handles vapor, never a mixture) and replace the turbine with a throttling device (expansion valve or capillary tube). The resulting cycle is the ideal vapor-compression refrigeration cycle.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.15: Ideal vapor-compression cycle

pool.q: In the ideal vapor-compression cycle, the refrigerant state at the compressor inlet (1), condenser outlet (3) and evaporator inlet (4) is, respectively:
o: saturated mixture; saturated liquid; slightly superheated vapor
saturated vapor; saturated vapor; saturated liquid
superheated vapor; compressed liquid; high-quality saturated mixture
saturated vapor; saturated liquid; low-quality saturated mixture
pool.e: Slides p.16–17: the refrigerant enters the compressor at state 1 as saturated vapor, leaves the condenser at state 3 as saturated liquid, and after the throttling valve enters the evaporator at state 4 as a low-quality saturated mixture (R-134a, 0.14–0.8 MPa: x₄ ≈ 0.32).
pool.s: states 1, 3, 4 of the ideal cycle (p.16–17)

pool.q: Of the four devices in the ideal vapor-compression cycle, which one exchanges work and which one is treated as adiabatic?
o: The condenser and evaporator exchange work; the throttling valve is adiabatic
All four devices exchange work; none is adiabatic
Only the compressor exchanges work; the compressor is treated as adiabatic
The compressor and throttling valve exchange work; the evaporator is adiabatic
pool.e: Slide p.19: all four are steady-flow devices; the condenser and evaporator involve no work; the compressor is approximated as adiabatic. The steady-flow equation (q_in − q_out) + (w_in − w_out) = h_e − h_i reduces to: compressor w_in = h₂ − h₁; condenser q_out = h₂ − h₃; evaporator q_in = h₁ − h₄.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.19: Ideal vapor-compression cycle

pool.q: Which expression is the COP of a REFRIGERATOR on the ideal vapor-compression cycle (state numbers as on the slide)?
pool.e: Slide p.20: COP_R = q_L/w_net,in = (h₁ − h₄)/(h₂ − h₁); COP_HP = q_H/w_net,in = (h₂ − h₃)/(h₂ − h₁). The expression (h₂ − h₃)/(h₂ − h₁) is the heat-pump COP; the inverted one is work over cooling effect.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.20: Ideal vapor-compression cycle

pool.q: Match correctly: the specific condenser output q_c (p.23) and the specific refrigerating capacity q₀ (p.25) are computed as
o: q_c = h₂ − h₃ and q₀ = h₁ − h₄
q_c = h₂ − h₁ and q₀ = h₃ − h₄
q_c = h₃ − h₄ and q₀ = h₂ − h₃
q_c = h₁ − h₄ and q₀ = h₂ − h₃
pool.e: Slide p.23: Q̇_c = (h₂ − h₃)·ṁ_R so q_c = h₂ − h₃ (horizontal segment 2–3 at high pressure). Slide p.25: Q̇₀ = (h₁ − h₄)·ṁ_R so q₀ = h₁ − h₄ (horizontal segment 4–1 at low pressure). Specific compressor work w_V = h₂ − h₁ (p.22).
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.23: Ideal vapor-compression cycle

pool.q: On the P–h diagram of the ideal vapor-compression cycle (slide p.18), which process is NOT a straight segment, and how is the heat exchanged in the condenser/evaporator represented?
o: Throttling 3→4 is a curve; heat is proportional to the area inside the cycle
Compression 1→2 is a curve; heat is proportional to the length of the horizontal segment
Evaporation 4→1 is a curve; heat is proportional to the pressure difference between the two states
Condensation 2→3 is a curve; heat is proportional to the length of the vertical segment
pool.e: Slide p.18: three of the four processes are straight lines (2→3 and 4→1 horizontal because isobaric, 3→4 vertical because h = const); compression 1→2 is a curve (isentropic) and the compression work is the difference h₂ − h₁. Heat in the condenser/evaporator is proportional to the length of the horizontal segment (enthalpy difference), not to an area. Qualitative description only: no numbers are read from the diagram.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.18: Ideal vapor-compression cycle

pool.q: What does slide p.26 say about the ideal refrigeration cycle compared with the real one?
o: The real cycle always has a higher COP than the ideal cycle
The ideal cycle assumes no losses occur; in practice this is not possible
The real cycle differs from the ideal one only in the throttling step
The ideal and real cycles coincide when R-134a is used
pool.e: Slide p.26: "In an ideal cycle, it is assumed that no losses occur in the system. In practice, this is not possible." The real-cycle log p–h figure (red) has slightly slanted horizontals (pressure drops), a condenser exit to the left of the saturated-liquid line (subcooling) and a compressor inlet to the right of the saturated-vapor line (superheat) (read qualitatively from the figure; Cengel §11-4 explains the details).
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.26: Real refrigeration cycle

pool.q: According to Cengel §11-4 (added), why is the system designed so that the refrigerant is slightly SUPERHEATED at the compressor inlet instead of saturated vapor?
o: To raise the specific compressor work and thereby raise the COP of the whole refrigeration cycle
So that the compressor can handle a liquid–vapor mixture of any quality without damage
So that the temperature at the end of compression stays below the temperature of the surrounding ambient air
To make sure the refrigerant is completely vaporized when it enters the compressor
pool.e: Cengel §11-4 (p.614): the state of the refrigerant is hard to control exactly, so the system is designed for slight superheat to be sure the fluid is completely vaporized; the cost is a larger specific volume and more compressor work (the long connecting line also adds pressure drop and heat gain). Slide p.26 only says losses exist; this detail comes from the book.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.26 + Cengel §11-4 (added from the book)

pool.q: In the refrigeration test rig on slide p.28, which two parts play the role of the throttling (expansion) device of the cycle?
o: The solenoid valve (8) and the process schematic (6)
The evaporation pressure controller (1) and the fan (3)
The capillary tube (7) and the expansion valve (9)
pool.e: Slide p.28 labels: 7 capillary tube, 9 expansion valve (the two kinds of throttling device named on p.15); 2 evaporator, 3 fan, 4 heater, 8 solenoid valve, 1 evaporation pressure controller. Slide p.27 labels the compressor (1), condenser (2) and receiver (3).
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.28: Refrigerating equipment

pool.q: According to slide p.29, which type of air-conditioning system is most used on turbine passenger jets?
pool.e: Slide p.29: air cycle air conditioning is the most used type on turbine passenger jets; vapor cycle is another type, more common on reciprocating aircraft.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.29: Cooling pack / ACM

pool.q: According to slide p.30, what does the cooling pack (air conditioning pack) use as refrigerant, and which machine combines a turbine and a compressor?
o: Secondary air from the APU; the primary heat exchanger
R-134a sealed in the pack; the engine's piston compressor
Water sprayed into the air stream; the ram-air pump
The air passing through and into the airplane; the Air Cycle Machine (A.C.M.)
pool.e: Slide p.30: the cooling pack is an air-cycle refrigeration system that uses the air passing through and into the airplane as the refrigerant, achieved by a combined turbine-and-compressor machine called the Air Cycle Machine (A.C.M.). Unlike the vapor-compression cycle (R-134a) there is no separate refrigerant.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.30: Cooling pack / ACM

pool.q: According to slide p.31, when the pack operates on the ground, what pulls the ram air across the heat exchangers?
o: The impeller fan powered by the turbine section of the ACM
The impeller fan powered by an electric motor of the pack
The dynamic pressure of the ram air from the aircraft's motion
The ACM compressor section drawing outside air directly
pool.e: Slide p.31: "When the pack is operating on the ground, ram air is pulled across the heat exchangers by the impeller fan powered by the turbine section of the air cycle machine". Slide p.35 adds: the turbine, compressor and fan are on the same shaft.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.31: Cooling pack / ACM

pool.q: In what order does the bleed air go through the first components of the cooling pack on slide p.31?
o: Ozone converter, then flow control valve
Flow control valve, then ozone converter
Primary heat exchanger, then ozone converter
ACM compressor, then flow control valve
pool.e: Slide p.31: bleed air enters the pack through the ozone converter (which turns the ozone in bleed air into oxygen by catalytic effect), then through the flow control valve that regulates the flow to the demand of the air-conditioning and cabin-pressurization systems; only then does it reach the primary heat exchanger (p.32). Note: the figure on p.30 has no ozone-converter label; only the text of p.31 mentions it.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.31: Cooling pack / ACM

pool.q: According to slides p.32–33, the order in which the bleed air passes the main components, from pack inlet to just before the water extractor, is:
o: Primary heat exchanger → ACM compressor → secondary heat exchanger
ACM compressor → primary heat exchanger → secondary heat exchanger
Primary heat exchanger → secondary heat exchanger → ACM compressor
Secondary heat exchanger → ACM compressor → primary heat exchanger
pool.e: Slide p.32: the flow-controlled bleed air goes "first" to the primary heat exchanger. Slide p.33: the partially cooled air goes to the compressor section of the ACM, then through the secondary heat exchanger. Cooling before compressing means the compressor receives cooler air (inference, not on the slide).
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.33: Cooling pack / ACM

pool.q: What does slide p.33 say the compressor section of the ACM does to the air passing through it, and by how much does the temperature change?
o: Compresses the air, raising pressure and temperature by about 30–40 °C
Keeps the pressure, heating the air by about 60 to 70 °C
Expands the air, lowering pressure and temperature by about 100 °C
Compresses the air, raising pressure but lowering temperature by about 30 to 40 °C
pool.e: Slide p.33: the compressor section "compresses the air and increases the pressure and temperature. The temperature rise ... is about 30 to 40 °C"; it is powered by the turbine section of the ACM. The 60–70 °C drop belongs to the secondary heat exchanger and the 100 °C drop to the primary one (p.32).
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.33: Cooling pack / ACM

pool.q: According to slide p.34, what is the purpose of the reheater that warms the air going to the turbine?
o: To supply heat to the cabin in cold weather
To increase the turbine efficiency (slide wording)
To bring the air below 0 °C before the turbine
To condense more water vapor out of the air before the turbine
pool.e: Slide p.34: "The dry air goes through the re heater to warm the air that goes to the turbine to increase the turbine efficiency." The slide does not explain the physical mechanism; none is added here. In the slide's text the water extractor is mentioned BEFORE the reheater: the air reaching the reheater is called dry air.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.34: Cooling pack / ACM

pool.q: According to slide p.35, what does the ACM turbine do to the air, and what is the speed of the shaft (carrying the compressor and the fan)?
o: Rapid expansion, lowering the temperature to 10 °C; 400 to 500 rpm
Rapid compression, raising the temperature to 150 °C; 40,000 to 50,000 rpm
Rapid expansion, lowering the temperature to −10 °C; 4,000 to 5,000 rpm
Rapid expansion, lowering the temperature to −10 °C; 40,000 to 50,000 rpm
pool.e: Slide p.35: rapid expansion and energy extraction across the turbine lowers the air temperature down to −10 °C and rotates the turbine wheel together with the wheels of the compressor and the fan (same shaft) at 40.000 to 50.000 rpm (the slide uses a dot as thousands separator). 40,000 rpm = 667 rev/s ≈ 4,189 rad/s.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.35: Cooling pack / ACM

pool.q: According to slide p.35, what is the cold air leaving the turbine used for when it flows across the "condenser"?
o: It cools the ram-air stream in the duct so that the impeller fan moves more air
It cools the warm air going to the water extractors below the dew point so excess moisture condenses into water
It heats the air going to the water extractors even more so that all the remaining water evaporates before the cabin
It cools the compressor section of the ACM with the cold air before that air enters the cabin
pool.e: Slide p.35: the cold air from the turbine outlet flowing across the condenser cools the warm air going to the water extractors below the "due point" (sic; dew point is meant), the excess moisture condenses into droplets and is removed by the centrifugal effect.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.35: Cooling pack / ACM

pool.q: How is the water collected from the two water extractors used, according to slide p.35?
o: Discharged straight overboard through the ram air exhaust
Sprayed into the ram air duct to improve the cooling efficiency of the heat exchangers
Fed to the storage tank of the potable-water system
Mixed back into the cabin supply air to keep humidity
pool.e: Slide p.35: the water collected from both water extractors is fed to spray nozzles in the ram air duct (the water spray nozzle in the p.30 figure) to improve the cooling efficiency of the heat exchangers.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.35: Cooling pack / ACM

pool.q: According to slide p.36, once the cold, dry air flows into the mixing box, what does the temperature mixing valve do?
o: Adds a small amount of cold water as needed to reach the desired cabin humidity
Vents some of the cold air overboard through the outflow valves to reach the desired cabin pressure
Reverses the air flow through the ACM so that the pack heats the cabin instead of cooling it
Adds a small amount of hot engine air as needed to reach the desired cabin temperature
pool.e: Slide p.36: a temperature mixing valve allows a small amount of hot engine air to be added to the cold, dry air as needed to reach the desired cabin air temperature; the air then flows into the cabin providing both pressurization and climate control.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.36: Cooling pack / ACM

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–52C (§11-8, added). How is the ideal-gas refrigeration cycle modified for aircraft cooling?
o: The compressor is removed and the engine turbine exhaust is used directly in the cabin without passing through any cooling stage at all
It becomes a closed cycle charged with R-134a, with a condenser, an evaporator and a receiver as in a household refrigerator
It becomes an open cycle: atmospheric air is compressed, cooled by the surrounding air, expanded in a turbine and routed directly to the cabin
The turbine is replaced by a throttling valve to reduce the weight and complexity of the on-board equipment, and the expanded air is recompressed
pool.e: Cengel §11-8 (p.629, Fig. 11–18): an open-cycle aircraft cooling system: atmospheric air is compressed, cooled by the surrounding air, expanded in a turbine and routed directly to the cabin. The book also notes that gas cycles have simple, light components, which suits aircraft. Slides p.30–36 show a real system that adds the ACM, water extractors, reheater and condenser: not part of the ideal model.
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–52C (§11-8, added from the book)

pool.q: Cengel Problem 11–5C (added). Why is the throttling valve of the ideal vapor-compression cycle not replaced by an isentropic turbine?
o: Because a turbine would lower the refrigeration capacity and raise the compressor work compared with the valve
Because no turbine can expand a liquid–vapor mixture isentropically, whatever the cost, so it is physically impossible
Because throttling is already an isentropic, reversible process, so the cycle is already optimal
The added benefits (more refrigeration capacity, less compressor work) cannot justify the added cost and complexity
pool.e: Cengel §11-3 (p.612): replacing the valve with a turbine would let the refrigerant enter the evaporator at state 4′ (lower enthalpy): refrigeration capacity increases and net work decreases; but it is "not practical since the added benefits cannot justify the added cost and complexity". For R-134a 0.14–0.8 MPa: COP rises from 3.97 to 5.06 (verify_m03.py).
pool.s: Cengel Problem 11–5C (added from the book)

Raising the evaporator pressure (T_sat from −18.8 to −5.4 °C) both raises q_L and lowers the compression work, so the COP rises by about 53 %. pool.q: According to slide p.32 the bleed air enters the pack at about 150 °C and drops by about 100 °C in the primary heat exchanger. The air temperature after the primary exchanger (derived, illustrative) is about:

pool.q: An ideal gas refrigeration cycle (reversed Brayton) with air (k = 1.4, constant c_p) has pressure ratio r_p = 2. The COP of the simple cycle (no regeneration) is:
pool.e: COP = q_L/w_net = 1/(r_p^((k−1)/k) − 1) = 1/(2^0.2857 − 1) = 1/0.2190 = 4.57 (Cengel §11-8, added from the book). 0.219 is not yet inverted; 1/(1 − r_p^(−0.2857)) = 5.57 is the heat-pump COP; 1/(r_p − 1) = 1.00 drops the exponent.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: gas-cycle COP

pool.q: An ideal gas refrigeration cycle (reversed Brayton) with air (k = 1.4, constant c_p) has pressure ratio r_p = 4. The COP of the simple cycle (no regeneration) is:
pool.e: COP = q_L/w_net = 1/(r_p^((k−1)/k) − 1) = 1/(4^0.2857 − 1) = 1/0.4860 = 2.06 (Cengel §11-8, added from the book). 0.486 is not yet inverted; 1/(1 − r_p^(−0.2857)) = 3.06 is the heat-pump COP; 1/(r_p − 1) = 0.33 drops the exponent.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: gas-cycle COP

pool.q: An ideal gas refrigeration cycle with air (k = 1.4): air enters the turbine at 40 °C, pressure ratio 3.0. The air temperature leaving the turbine (°C) is:
pool.e: T₄ = T₃/r_p^((k−1)/k) = 313.15/3.0^0.2857 = 313.15/1.3687 = 228.8 K = −44.4 °C. Using °C in the formula gives 29; dividing T by r_p gives −169; multiplying (compression instead of expansion) gives 155 °C.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: turbine outlet temperature of the gas cycle

pool.q: An ideal gas refrigeration cycle with air (k = 1.4): air enters the turbine at 50 °C, pressure ratio 2.5. The air temperature leaving the turbine (°C) is:
pool.e: T₄ = T₃/r_p^((k−1)/k) = 323.15/2.5^0.2857 = 323.15/1.2993 = 248.7 K = −24.4 °C. Using °C in the formula gives 38; dividing T by r_p gives −144; multiplying (compression instead of expansion) gives 147 °C.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: turbine outlet temperature of the gas cycle

pool.q: A regenerative gas refrigeration cycle with air (k = 1.4, c_p = 1.005): compressor inlet 0 °C, r_p = 3; after the heat sink 35 °C, after the regenerator −10 °C (turbine inlet). Compressor and turbine are isentropic. The mass flow rate for a 15 kW refrigeration load (kg/s) is:
pool.e: T₅ = T₄/3^0.2857 = 263.15/1.3687 = 192.3 K. Regenerator: T₆ = T₁ − (T₃ − T₄) = 273.15 − 45 = 228.15 K. q_L = c_p(T₆ − T₅) = 1.005·(228.15 − 192.3) = 36.07 kJ/kg ⇒ ṁ = 15/36.07 = 0.416 kg/s. Using T₁ − T₅ (ignoring the regenerator) gives 0.185; dividing by the net work 30.0 kJ/kg gives 0.500; using T₄ − T₅ instead of T₆ − T₅ gives 0.211.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: regenerative gas refrigeration cycle

pool.q: A simple gas refrigeration cycle with air (k = 1.4): compressor inlet 10 °C, turbine inlet 45 °C, r_p = 3, isentropic efficiency 80 % for the compressor and 85 % for the turbine. The COP of the cycle is:
pool.e: x = 3^0.2857 = 1.3687. Real compression: T₂ = T₁ + T₁(x − 1)/η_c = 413.7 K; real expansion: T₄ = T₃ − η_t(T₃ − T₃/x) = 245.3 K. q_L = c_p(T₁ − T₄) = 38.04; w_c = 131.16; w_t = 73.22; w_net = 57.95 kJ/kg ⇒ COP = 0.66. The ideal cycle gives 2.71; ignoring the turbine work gives 0.29; multiplying the efficiencies into the ideal COP gives 1.84 (wrong: efficiencies act differently on numerator and denominator).
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: gas cycle with component efficiencies

pool.q: Air at 25 °C and 60 % relative humidity. The dew point is about (Tables A-4/A-5), in °C:
pool.e: P_g@25 °C = 3.170 kPa (A-4) ⇒ P_v = φ·P_g = 0.6·3.170 = 1.902 kPa. Dew point = T_sat@P_v = 16.6 °C (A-5, linear interpolation). Multiplying φ by the temperature gives 15.0 (wrong: φ is a pressure ratio); the dew point is not the air temperature when φ < 1; taking P_v = φ·100 kPa gives 85.5 °C. Slide p.35 writes "due point": dew point is meant.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.35 (dew point) + Cengel §14-3 (added from the book)

pool.q: Air at 30 °C and 50 % relative humidity. The dew point is about (Tables A-4/A-5), in °C:
pool.e: P_g@30 °C = 4.247 kPa (A-4) ⇒ P_v = φ·P_g = 0.5·4.247 = 2.123 kPa. Dew point = T_sat@P_v = 18.4 °C (A-5, linear interpolation). Multiplying φ by the temperature gives 15.0 (wrong: φ is a pressure ratio); the dew point is not the air temperature when φ < 1; taking P_v = φ·100 kPa gives 81.3 °C. Slide p.35 writes "due point": dew point is meant.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.35 (dew point) + Cengel §14-3 (added from the book)

pool.q: An R-134a refrigeration system on the ideal vapor-compression cycle between 240 kPa and 1200 kPa has a refrigeration rate of 20 kW. The heat rejected by the condenser to the environment Q̇_H (kW) is:
pool.e: ṁ = Q̇_L/(h₁ − h₄) = 20/129.51 = 0.1544 kg/s; Q̇_H = ṁ(h₂ − h₃) = 0.1544·163.08 = 25.2 kW (= Q̇_L + Ẇ = 20 + 5.2). 20 is Q̇_L; 77.2 multiplies by the COP; 5.2 is only the compressor power.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: condenser heat rejection from the cooling load

pool.q: An R-134a refrigeration system on the ideal vapor-compression cycle between 320 kPa and 1400 kPa has a refrigeration rate of 30 kW. The heat rejected by the condenser to the environment Q̇_H (kW) is:
pool.e: ṁ = Q̇_L/(h₁ − h₄) = 30/124.66 = 0.2407 kg/s; Q̇_H = ṁ(h₂ − h₃) = 0.2407·155.34 = 37.4 kW (= Q̇_L + Ẇ = 30 + 7.4). 30 is Q̇_L; 121.9 multiplies by the COP; 7.4 is only the compressor power.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: condenser heat rejection from the cooling load

pool.q: In the ideal R-134a vapor-compression cycle between 140 kPa and 800 kPa, the throttling valve is replaced by an isentropic turbine (expanding saturated liquid from 800 kPa to 140 kPa and delivering work that offsets the compressor). The new COP exceeds the old one by about:
pool.e: s₃ = s_f@800 kPa; x₄ₛ = 0.292; h₄ₛ = 88.94 kJ/kg (versus h₄ = 95.47). New q_L = h₁ − h₄ₛ = 150.22; new w = (h₂ − h₁) − (h₃ − h₄ₛ) = 29.70 ⇒ new COP = 5.06 versus 3.97: up 27.5 %. 4.5 % is only the increase of q_L; 18.0 % is turbine work over compressor work.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: turbine instead of the throttling valve

pool.q: In the ideal R-134a vapor-compression cycle between 200 kPa and 1000 kPa, the throttling valve is replaced by an isentropic turbine (expanding saturated liquid from 1000 kPa to 200 kPa and delivering work that offsets the compressor). The new COP exceeds the old one by about:
pool.e: s₃ = s_f@1000 kPa; x₄ₛ = 0.303; h₄ₛ = 100.86 kJ/kg (versus h₄ = 107.32). New q_L = h₁ − h₄ₛ = 143.60; new w = (h₂ − h₁) − (h₃ − h₄ₛ) = 27.11 ⇒ new COP = 5.30 versus 4.09: up 29.6 %. 4.7 % is only the increase of q_L; 19.2 % is turbine work over compressor work.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: turbine instead of the throttling valve

pool.q: Ideal R-134a vapor-compression cycle between 200 kPa and 1000 kPa (T_sat = −10.09 °C and 39.37 °C). The ratio of its COP to that of a reversed Carnot cycle between those saturation temperatures is about:
pool.e: COP_cycle = 4.09; COP_Carnot = T_L/(T_H − T_L) = 263.06/49.46 = 5.32 ⇒ ratio = 0.77 (< 1 because of irreversible throttling and superheated-vapor compression). 1.30 is the inverted ratio; 0.65 divides by the Carnot heat-pump COP; 21.73 divides by T_H/T_L − 1 not yet inverted.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: COP ratio actual/Carnot

pool.q: Ideal R-134a vapor-compression cycle between 100 kPa and 800 kPa (T_sat = −26.37 °C and 31.31 °C). The ratio of its COP to that of a reversed Carnot cycle between those saturation temperatures is about:
pool.e: COP_cycle = 3.21; COP_Carnot = T_L/(T_H − T_L) = 246.78/57.68 = 4.28 ⇒ ratio = 0.75 (< 1 because of irreversible throttling and superheated-vapor compression). 1.33 is the inverted ratio; 0.61 divides by the Carnot heat-pump COP; 13.75 divides by T_H/T_L − 1 not yet inverted.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: COP ratio actual/Carnot

pool.q: Slide p.33 gives the temperature rise through the ACM compressor as about 30–40 °C and (derived from p.32) the air entering it as about 50 °C; the slide gives NO pressure ratio. Illustration: assume isentropic compression, k = 1.4, a 35 K rise. The compressor pressure ratio would be about:
pool.e: T₂/T₁ = (323.15 + 35)/323.15 = 1.1083; isentropic: r_p = (T₂/T₁)^(k/(k−1)) = 1.1083^3.5 = 1.43. This is only an illustration (the slides give no number; a real, lossy compressor needs a different pressure ratio for the same rise). 1.108 is the temperature ratio; 1.030 uses the inverted exponent (k−1)/k.
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.32–33 + Cengel §11-8 (illustration, isentropic assumption)

pool.q: Slides p.34–35: the air enters the ACM turbine at about 10–20 °C (take 15 °C) and leaves at −10 °C; the slides give NO expansion ratio. Illustration: assume isentropic expansion, k = 1.4. The pressure ratio across the turbine would be about:
pool.e: T₁/T₂ = 288.15/263.15 = 1.0950; r_p = (T₁/T₂)^(k/(k−1)) = 1.0950^3.5 = 1.37. Illustration under the isentropic assumption: a real, lossy turbine needs a larger ratio for the same temperature drop. 1.095 is the temperature ratio; 1.026 uses the exponent (k−1)/k; 1.5 uses °C (15/10).
pool.s: Slide Ch.3 p.34–35 + Cengel §11-8 (illustration, isentropic assumption)

pool.q: An air conditioner of 3.5 tons (1 ton = 211 kJ/min) with COP = 4.0 runs continuously to hold a constant room temperature. The heat it rejects outdoors Q̇_H (kW) is:
pool.e: Q̇_L = 3.5·211/60 = 12.31 kW (equal to the heat leaking into the room at constant temperature); Ẇ = Q̇_L/COP = 3.08 kW; Q̇_H = Q̇_L + Ẇ = 15.39 kW. 12.31 is only the cooling load; 3.08 is only the electric power; 49.2 multiplies by COP.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: tons, COP and rejected heat

pool.q: R-134a enters the compressor at 0.14 MPa, −10 °C (h₁ = 246.36 kJ/kg), is compressed to 0.8 MPa with η_c = 80 % (h₂ₛ = 284.21 kJ/kg); it leaves the condenser as liquid at 30 °C (h₃ ≅ 93.58 kJ/kg); ṁ = 0.05 kg/s. The heat rejected in the condenser Q̇_H (kW) is:
pool.e: h₂ = h₁ + (h₂ₛ − h₁)/η_c = 293.67 kJ/kg (the real state, not h₂ₛ); Q̇_H = ṁ(h₂ − h₃) = 0.05·(293.67 − 93.58) = 10.00 kW (= Q̇_L + Ẇ = 7.64 + 2.37). 9.53 uses h₂ₛ; 7.64 is Q̇_L; 2.37 is the compressor power.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: heat rejection of the actual cycle

pool.q: R-134a enters the compressor at 0.14 MPa, −10 °C (h₁ = 246.36 kJ/kg), is compressed to 1.0 MPa with η_c = 75 % (h₂ₛ = 289.25 kJ/kg); it leaves the condenser as liquid at 28 °C (h₃ ≅ 90.69 kJ/kg); ṁ = 0.04 kg/s. The heat rejected in the condenser Q̇_H (kW) is:
pool.e: h₂ = h₁ + (h₂ₛ − h₁)/η_c = 303.55 kJ/kg (the real state, not h₂ₛ); Q̇_H = ṁ(h₂ − h₃) = 0.04·(303.55 − 90.69) = 8.51 kW (= Q̇_L + Ẇ = 6.23 + 2.29). 7.94 uses h₂ₛ; 6.23 is Q̇_L; 2.29 is the compressor power.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: heat rejection of the actual cycle

pool.q: An ideal R-134a vapor-compression cycle has a 800 kPa condenser pressure. When the evaporator pressure rises from 140 to 200 kPa (saturation temperature from −18.77 to −10.09 °C), by how many percent does the COP rise on average per °C?
pool.e: COP(140 kPa) = 3.966, COP(200 kPa) = 5.169: up 30.3 % over 8.68 °C ⇒ 3.5 %/°C: inside the 2–4 % per °C that Cengel §11-3 gives as a rule of thumb (added). 30.3 is the total rise, not yet divided by the number of °C; 0.139 is the absolute rise per °C; 13.9 mixes the units.
pool.s: Added – generated from the type: COP gain per degree of evaporating temperature

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.15–16 (Cengel Example 15–1): C₈H₁₈ + 20(O₂ + 3.76 N₂) → x CO₂ + y H₂O + z O₂ + w N₂. The coefficients (x; y; z; w) of the products are:
pool.e: C: x = 8. H: 18 = 2y → y = 9. O: 40 = 2x + y + 2z = 25 + 2z → z = 7.5. N₂: w = 20 × 3.76 = 75.2. The set (8; 18; 7.5; 75.2) forgets that each H₂O takes 2 H atoms (y = 18/2); (8; 9; 12.5; 75.2) takes z as the theoretical O₂ 12.5 instead of the excess 20 − 12.5 = 7.5; (8; 9; 7.5; 95.2) confuses the moles of air (95.2) with the moles of N₂.
pool.s: Slide Ch.4 p.15–16 = Cengel Ex 15-1

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.27–32 (Cengel Example 15–2): ethane C₂H₆ is burned completely with 20 percent excess air at a total pressure of 100 kPa; products: 2 CO₂ + 3 H₂O + 0.7 O₂ + 15.79 N₂. The dew-point temperature of the products (Table A-5) is about:
pool.e: P_v = 3/21.49 × 100 = 13.96 kPa; T_dp = T_sat@13.96 kPa = 52.3 °C (A-5 interpolation, slide 52.3; IAPWS 52.5 °C). 99.6 °C is T_sat at the TOTAL pressure 100 kPa, not at the partial pressure of the vapor. 55.5 °C uses the dry product moles (without the H₂O) as the denominator of P_v. 49.1 °C takes P_v = N_v / N_O₂,th × 10 kPa (divides by moles of fuel).
pool.s: Slide Ch.4 p.27–32 = Cengel Ex 15-2

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.33–36 (Cengel Example 15–4): octane burned with dry air, dry products (mol %): 10.02 CO₂; 0.88 CO; 5.62 O₂; 83.48 N₂. The equation per kmol of fuel has 16.32 kmol O₂ in the air. The air–fuel ratio AF (kg/kg, M_air = 29) is about:
pool.e: AF = (16.32 × 4.76 kmol)(29 kg/kmol)/[(8)(12) + (9)(2)] = 2,252.8/114 = 19.76 kg/kg (slide p.36; with the unrounded x = 1.3625: 19.73). 16.32 kg/kg is the kmol O₂ per kmol fuel, not yet multiplied by 4.76 and the molar masses. 15.14 kg/kg is the AF of theoretical combustion (12.5 kmol O₂), not of the actual process. 4.58 kg/kg drops the N₂ of the air (only O₂: 16.32 × 32)/114.
pool.s: Slide Ch.4 p.36 = Cengel Ex 15-4

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.36–37 (Cengel Example 15–4): the actual air is 16.32 kmol O₂ per kmol of octane; the theoretical air needs a_th = 12.5 kmol O₂. The percentage of theoretical air used is:
pool.e: 16.32/12.5 = 1.306 = 130.6 % (slide prints 131 %, i.e. 31 percent excess air); percent theoretical air = N_air,act/N_air,th = m_air,act/m_air,th because the molar mass is the same; 100 % = theoretical combustion. 31.0 % is the percent EXCESS air (131 % − 100 %). 76.6 % inverts the ratio (theoretical/actual). 23.4 % divides the excess by the actual amount ((16.32 − 12.5)/16.32).
pool.s: Slide Ch.4 p.36–37 = Cengel Ex 15-4

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.38–39 (Cengel Example 15–4): the products per kmol of octane total 82.53 kmol, of which 9 kmol is H₂O. When cooled to 25 °C at 100 kPa (P_sat = 3.1698 kPa) the condensed water N_w (kmol per kmol of fuel) is:
pool.e: (9 − N_w)/(82.53 − N_w) = 0.031698 → N_w = (9 − 0.031698 × 82.53)/(1 − 0.031698) = 6.59 kmol, i.e. 73 % of the vapor (slide p.39: 6.59 kmol, 73 %). 2.41 kmol is the vapor REMAINING (9 − N_w). 6.38 kmol forgets that the denominator also shrinks by N_w: 9 − 0.031698 × 82.53. 9.00 kmol assumes all 9 kmol condense.
pool.s: Slide Ch.4 p.38–39 = Cengel Ex 15-4

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.54 (Cengel Example 15–5): the enthalpy of combustion of liquid octane C₈H₁₈ at 25 °C, 1 atm, liquid water in the products, is −5,471,000 kJ/kmol. Per kilogram of fuel (M = 114.231 kg/kmol) it is:
pool.e: h̄_C/M = −5,470,680/114.231 = −47,891 kJ/kg (slide −47,891); the A-27 higher heating value is 47,890 kJ/kg because the water is liquid. −5,471,000 kJ/kg not yet divided by the molar mass (still kJ/kmol). 47,891 kJ/kg wrong sign: the enthalpy of combustion of an exothermic reaction is NEGATIVE. −48,255 kJ/kg uses GASEOUS octane (−5,512,200 kJ/kmol), not liquid octane.
pool.s: Slide Ch.4 p.54 = Cengel Ex 15-5

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–13. Methane (CH₄) is burned with the stoichiometric amount of air. Assuming complete combustion, the air–fuel ratio AF (mass basis) is:
pool.e: a_th = 2.00 kmol O₂ per kmol fuel (O₂ balance); actual O₂ = 1.00 × a_th = 2.00; air = 4.76 × 2.00 = 9.52 kmol; AF = 9.52 × 29/16.00 = 17.25 kg/kg. The fuel–air ratio FA = 1/AF = 0.058 is the second answer of the statement. 4.0 kg/kg drops the N₂ of the air (O₂ only). 9.5 kg/kg is the AF on a mole basis (kmol air per kmol fuel), not converted to mass. 0.1 kg/kg is the fuel–air ratio FA = 1/AF.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–13

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–14. Propane (C₃H₈) is burned with 75 percent excess air. Assuming complete combustion, the air–fuel ratio is:
pool.e: a_th = 5.00 kmol O₂ per kmol fuel (O₂ balance); actual O₂ = 1.75 × a_th = 8.75; air = 4.76 × 8.75 = 41.65 kmol; AF = 41.65 × 29/44.00 = 27.45 kg/kg (printed answer 27.5). 6.4 kg/kg drops the N₂ of the air (O₂ only). 41.6 kg/kg is the AF on a mole basis (kmol air per kmol fuel), not converted to mass. 15.7 kg/kg uses theoretical air (λ = 1) and ignores the excess. 11.8 kg/kg reads 75 percent excess air as 75 percent theoretical air.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–14

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–15. Acetylene (C₂H₂) is burned with the stoichiometric amount of air, complete combustion. The air–fuel ratio on a mass basis and on a mole basis is:
pool.e: C₂H₂ + 2.5(O₂ + 3.76 N₂) → 2 CO₂ + H₂O + 9.4 N₂: air = 2.5 × 4.76 = 11.9 kmol per kmol fuel (mole AF); mass AF = 11.9 × 29/26 = 13.3 kg/kg. The second option drops the N₂ of the air; the swapped option mixes the units; the last option halves the values by misreading the coefficient of C₂H₂.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–15

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–16. One kmol of ethane (C₂H₆) is burned with an unknown amount of air. The product analysis shows complete combustion and 3 kmol of free O₂ in the products. The air–fuel ratio AF (kg/kg) is:
pool.e: O₂ in = a_th + 3 = 3.5 + 3 = 6.5 kmol (3 kmol O₂ left over, 3 kmol H₂O need 1.5 and CO₂ needs 2); air = 6.5 × 4.76 = 30.94 kmol; AF = 30.94 × 29/30 = 29.9 kg/kg; percent theoretical air = 6.5/3.5 = 185.7 % (part b of the book). 13.8 kg/kg takes the 3 kmol of free O₂ as all the O₂ supplied. 16.1 kg/kg uses the theoretical air a_th = 3.5 and ignores the excess. 30.9 kg/kg is the AF on a mole basis.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–16

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–17E (part a). Ethylene (C₂H₄) is burned with 200 percent theoretical air, complete combustion, total pressure 14.5 psia. The air–fuel ratio (lbm air per lbm fuel) is:
pool.e: C₂H₄ + 3(O₂ + 3.76 N₂) needs a_th = 3; 200 % → 6 kmol O₂ → air 6 × 4.76 = 28.56 kmol; AF = 28.56 × 29/28 = 29.6 (printed answer 29.6). A mass ratio does not depend on the unit system. 6.9 lbm/lbm drops the N₂ of the air (O₂ only). 28.6 lbm/lbm is the AF on a mole basis (kmol air per kmol fuel), not converted to mass. 14.8 lbm/lbm uses theoretical air (λ = 1) and ignores the excess.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–17E (part a)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–18 (part b). Propylene (C₃H₆) is burned with 50 percent excess air, complete combustion, total pressure 105 kPa. The temperature at which the water vapor in the products starts to condense (Table A-5) is about:
pool.e: C₃H₆ + 6.75(O₂ + 3.76 N₂) → 3 CO₂ + 3 H₂O + 2.25 O₂ + 25.38 N₂; N_prod = 33.63 kmol; P_v = 3/33.63 × 105 = 9.37 kPa → T_dp = T_sat = 44.4 °C (A-5 interpolation; IAPWS 44.5 °C). AF = 22.2 kg/kg (part a). 100.9 °C is T_sat at the total pressure of 105 kPa. 46.3 °C leaves the H₂O out of the total product moles. 31.4 °C uses the wrong O₂ supply (4.5 instead of 6.75 kmol).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–18 (part b)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–19. Propyl alcohol (C₃H₇OH) is burned with 50 percent excess air. Write the balanced equation for complete combustion and determine the air-to-fuel ratio.
pool.e: a_th = 4.50 kmol O₂ per kmol fuel (O₂ balance); actual O₂ = 1.50 × a_th = 6.75; air = 4.76 × 6.75 = 32.13 kmol; AF = 32.13 × 29/60.00 = 15.53 kg/kg (printed answer 15.5). The fuel contains O, so a_th = 3 + 2 − 0.5 = 4.5 (the O in the fuel supplies some of the oxygen). 3.6 kg/kg drops the N₂ of the air (O₂ only). 32.1 kg/kg is the AF on a mole basis (kmol air per kmol fuel), not converted to mass. 10.4 kg/kg uses theoretical air (λ = 1) and ignores the excess. 5.2 kg/kg reads 50 percent excess air as 50 percent theoretical air.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–19

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–20. Butane (C₄H₁₀) is burned in 200 percent theoretical air, complete combustion. How many kmol of water must be sprayed into the combustion chamber per kmol of fuel if the products are to have a dew-point temperature of 60 °C at a product pressure of 100 kPa? (P_sat@60 °C = 19.947 kPa).
pool.e: Products before spraying: 4 CO₂ + 5 H₂O + 6.5 O₂ + 48.88 N₂ = 64.38 kmol. Dew point 60 °C ⇒ P_v = 19.947 kPa, y_v = 0.19947. (5 + w)/(64.38 + w) = 0.19947 ⇒ w = (12.842 − 5)/(1 − 0.19947) = 9.80 kmol water per kmol fuel. 12.84 kmol takes N_v = (P_sat/P) N_prod without subtracting the 5 kmol of vapor already present. 7.84 kmol forgets that the sprayed water also increases N_prod (the denominator). 14.80 kmol is the total vapor (5 + w), not the amount sprayed.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–20

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–21. A fuel mixture of 20 percent by mass methane (CH₄) and 80 percent by mass ethanol (C₂H₆O) is burned completely with theoretical air. The total fuel flow rate is 31 kg/s. The required air flow rate is:
pool.e: For 100 kg of fuel: 20/16 = 1.25 kmol CH₄ needing 2 O₂ per kmol and 80/46 = 1.739 kmol C₂H₆O needing 3 O₂ per kmol ⇒ O₂ = 2.5 + 5.217 = 7.717 kmol; air = 36.73 kmol × 29 = 1,065.3 kg ⇒ AF = 10.653 kg/kg ⇒ ṁ_air = 10.653 × 31 = 330.2 kg/s (printed answer 330 kg/s). 535 kg/s treats all 31 kg/s as methane. 279 kg/s treats all 31 kg/s as ethanol. 407 kg/s averages the two AF values 50–50 instead of by mass fractions.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–21

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–22 (part b). Octane (C₈H₁₈) is burned with 250 percent theoretical air (air enters at 25 °C), complete combustion, total pressure 1 atm = 101.325 kPa. The dew-point temperature of the products (A-5) is about:
pool.e: Products: 8 CO₂ + 9 H₂O + 18.75 O₂ + 117.5 N₂ = 153.25 kmol; P_v = 9/153.25 × 101.325 = 5.95 kPa → T_dp ≈ 35.7 °C (A-5 interpolation; IAPWS 36.0 °C). AF = 37.8 kg/kg (part a). 100.0 °C is T_sat at the total pressure. 36.8 °C leaves the H₂O out of the total moles. 52.7 °C uses the products of theoretical combustion (no excess air).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–22 (part b)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–23. Gasoline (assumed C₈H₁₈) is burned steadily with air in a jet engine. If the air–fuel ratio is 18 kg air/kg fuel, the percentage of theoretical air used is:
pool.e: Theoretical AF of octane = 12.5 × 4.76 × 29/114 = 15.14 kg/kg; % theoretical = 18/15.14 = 118.9 % (≈ 19 % excess). 18.9 % is the percent EXCESS air, not percent theoretical. 84.1 % inverts the ratio. 74.4 % uses the AF of Example 15–1 (24.2) in place of the theoretical AF.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–23

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–24. In a combustion chamber, ethane (C₂H₆) is burned at a rate of 8 kg/h with air entering at a rate of 176 kg/h. The percentage of EXCESS air is:
pool.e: Actual AF = 176/8 = 22; theoretical AF of ethane (a_th = 3.5): 3.5 × 4.76 × 29/30 = 16.10; percent theoretical air = 22/16.10 = 136.6 % ⇒ excess 36.6 % (printed answer 37 %). 137 % is the percent THEORETICAL air (137 %), not yet minus 100 %. 27 % divides by the actual AF instead of by the theoretical AF. 22 % is the actual AF (22 kg/kg).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–24

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–25 (part b). One kilogram of butane (C₄H₁₀) is burned with 25 kg of air at 30 °C and 90 kPa. Complete combustion, product pressure 90 kPa. The dew-point temperature of the products (A-5) is about:
pool.e: Actual AF = 25; theoretical AF of butane = 6.5 × 4.76 × 29/58 = 15.47 ⇒ 161.6 % theoretical (part a; printed answer of the English-unit twin 15–26E: 161 %). Products: 4 CO₂ + 5 H₂O + 4.00 O₂ + 39.50 N₂ = 52.50 kmol; P_v = 5/52.50 × 90 = 8.57 kPa → T_dp ≈ 42.7 °C (IAPWS 42.8 °C). 96.5 °C is T_sat at the total pressure of 90 kPa. 51.5 °C uses the product moles of theoretical combustion. 30.0 °C takes the air inlet temperature as the dew point.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–25 (part b)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–27. A certain natural gas has the volumetric analysis 65 percent CH₄, 8 percent H₂, 18 percent N₂, 3 percent O₂ and 6 percent CO₂. It is burned completely with the stoichiometric amount of dry air. The air–fuel ratio is:
pool.e: Per kmol of fuel: O₂ needed = 0.65×2 + 0.08×0.5 − 0.03 = 1.310 kmol (the CO₂ and N₂ of the fuel are inert); air = 6.236 kmol; fuel molar mass = 0.65×16 + 0.08×2 + 0.18×28 + 0.03×32 + 0.06×44 = 19.20 kg/kmol ⇒ AF = 6.236 × 29/19.20 = 9.42 kg/kg. 6.24 kg/kg is the AF on a mole basis (kmol/kmol). 17.52 kg/kg uses only the two combustibles (CH₄ + H₂) as the fuel mass. 10.83 kg/kg forgets the O₂ already in the fuel and the inert N₂ in the AF.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–27

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–29 (part a). A gaseous fuel with a volumetric analysis of 60 percent CH₄, 30 percent H₂ and 10 percent N₂ is burned to completion with 130 percent theoretical air. The air–fuel ratio is:
pool.e: Per kmol of fuel: a_th = 0.6×2 + 0.3×0.5 = 1.35 kmol O₂; actual O₂ = 1.3 × 1.35 = 1.755; air = 8.35 kmol; M = 0.6×16 + 0.3×2 + 0.1×28 = 13.0 kg/kmol ⇒ AF = 8.35 × 29/13.0 = 18.64 kg/kg (printed answer 18.6). 14.3 kg/kg ignores the 30 percent excess. 8.4 kg/kg is the AF on a mole basis. 23.8 kg/kg does not count the mass of the 10 % inert N₂ of the fuel.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–29 (part a)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–29 (part b). The same fuel (60 % CH₄, 30 % H₂, 10 % N₂) burns with 130 percent theoretical air; the products are cooled to 20 °C at 1 atm (P_sat@20 °C = 2.3392 kPa). The fraction of the water vapor that condenses is:
pool.e: Products: N_v = 1.50, N_prod = 9.20 kmol; (N_v − N_w)/(N_prod − N_w) = 2.3392/101.325 ⇒ N_w = 1.318 kmol = 87.9 % (printed answer 88 %). 16 % is the mole fraction of vapor in the products, not the condensed fraction. 12 % is the vapor REMAINING. 98 % assumes the remaining vapor mole fraction P_sat/P = 2.3 % is the amount left and condenses the rest.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–29 (part b)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–31. A certain coal has the mass analysis 82 percent C, 5 percent H₂O, 2 percent H₂, 1 percent O₂ and 10 percent ash. The coal is burned with 50 percent excess air. The air–fuel ratio (kg air/kg coal) is:
pool.e: For 100 kg of coal: C = 82/12 = 6.833 kmol, H₂ = 2/2 = 1 kmol, O₂ = 1/32 = 0.0312 kmol; H₂O and ash are inert (their mass still counts as coal). a_th = C + H₂/2 − O₂ = 7.302 kmol; actual O₂ = 1.5 × 7.302; air = 52.14 kmol = 1,512.0 kg ⇒ AF = 15.12 kg/kg (printed answer 15.1). 15.2 kg/kg ignores the O₂ already in the coal. 17.4 kg/kg divides by only the C + H₂ + O₂ mass (87 kg) instead of the 100 kg of coal. 10.1 kg/kg drops the 50 % excess air.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–31

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–33 (part b). Carbon (C) is burned with dry air. The volumetric analysis of the products is 10.06 percent CO₂, 0.42 percent CO, 10.69 percent O₂ and 78.83 percent N₂. The percentage of theoretical air used is:
pool.e: For 100 kmol of dry products: a = 78.83/3.76 = 20.965 kmol O₂; x C = 10.06 + 0.42 = 10.48 kmol; a_th = 1 kmol O₂ per kmol C ⇒ % = a/(x·1) = 20.965/10.48 = 200.1 % (AF = 23.0 kg/kg; O₂ check gap 0.005). 100 % is the percent excess air. 50 % inverts the ratio. 300 % adds 100 % by mistake.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–33 (part b)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–34 (part a). Methane (CH₄) is burned with dry air. The volumetric analysis of the products on a dry basis is 5.20 percent CO₂, 0.33 percent CO, 11.24 percent O₂ and 83.23 percent N₂. The air–fuel ratio (kg/kg) is:
pool.e: 100 kmol of dry products: a = 83.23/3.76 = 22.136; C: x = 5.20 + 0.33 = 5.53 kmol CH₄; air per kmol fuel = 4.76 × 4.003 = 19.05 kmol; AF = 19.05 × 29/16 = 34.5 kg/kg; % theoretical = 4.003/2 = 200.1 % (printed answers 34.5 and 200 %). 19.1 kg/kg is the AF on a mole basis. 17.3 kg/kg is the theoretical AF of methane (17.3). 8.0 kg/kg drops the N₂ of the air (O₂ only).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–34 (part a)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–42. Determine the enthalpy of combustion of methane (CH₄) at 25 °C and 1 atm using the enthalpy of formation data of Table A-26, assuming the water in the products is liquid. Compare with Table A-27. The enthalpy of combustion (kJ/kmol CH₄) is:
pool.e: CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O(ℓ): h̄_C = (1)(−393,520) + (2)(−285,830) − (1)(−74,850) = −890,330 kJ/kmol (printed answer −890,330). Check with A-27: HHV = 55,530 kJ/kg × 16.043 = 890,868 kJ/kmol (difference 0.06 %). 802,310 kJ/kmol wrong sign. −802,310 kJ/kmol uses H₂O vapor (−241,820), so it is the LHV, not the enthalpy of combustion with liquid water. −965,180 kJ/kmol forgets to subtract the enthalpy of formation of the fuel (−74,850).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–42

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–44 (repeat of 15–42 for gaseous ethane C₂H₆). The enthalpy of combustion of gaseous ethane at 25 °C and 1 atm with liquid water in the products (A-26) is:
pool.e: C₂H₆ + 3.5 O₂ → 2 CO₂ + 3 H₂O(ℓ): h̄_C = 2(−393,520) + 3(−285,830) − (−84,680) = −1,559,850 kJ/kmol = −51,874 kJ/kg. A-27: HHV = 51,900 × 30.07 = 1,560,633 kJ/kmol (difference 0.05 %); the book prints no answer. −1,427,820 kJ/kmol uses H₂O vapor (LHV). −779,925 kJ/kmol writes the equation for 1/2 kmol of C₂H₆ (halves the CO₂ coefficient). −1,729,210 kJ/kmol adds instead of subtracting the fuel enthalpy of formation (twice).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–44

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–49. Methane (CH₄) is burned completely with the stoichiometric amount of air in a steady-flow process. Reactants and products are both at 25 °C and 1 atm and the water in the products is liquid. The heat transferred out of the chamber per kmol of fuel is:
pool.e: Q = H_prod − H_react = h̄_C = −890,330 kJ/kmol: heat released 890,330 kJ/kmol CH₄ (printed answer 890,330). With 100 percent excess air still at 25 °C the result is unchanged: the extra N₂ and O₂ enter and leave at the same standard state with h̄_f° = 0 (second half of the statement). 802,310 kJ/kmol computed with H₂O vapor (LHV). 55,496 kJ/kmol divided by the molar mass (kJ/kg, not kJ/kmol). −890,330 kJ/kmol heat INTO the chamber (wrong sign): the reaction is exothermic.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–49

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–50. Hydrogen (H₂) is burned completely with the stoichiometric amount of air in a steady-flow process; reactants and products at 25 °C and 1 atm, liquid water. The heat released from the chamber per KILOGRAM of hydrogen (A-26; M = 2.016 kg/kmol) is:
pool.e: H₂ + 1/2 O₂ → H₂O(ℓ): h̄_C = h̄_f°(H₂O ℓ) = −285,830 kJ/kmol ⇒ 141,781 kJ/kg. Check with A-27: HHV(H₂) = 141,800 kJ/kg (difference 0.014 %); LHV = 120,000. 50 % excess air does not change the result when all streams are at 25 °C. 285,830 kJ/kg is kJ per kmol, not divided by M. 119,950 kJ/kg computed with H₂O vapor (LHV; A-27 prints 120,000). 15,866 kJ/kg divides by the molar mass of H₂O (18.015) instead of that of H₂.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–50

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–104 (part c). A gaseous fuel mixture of 30 percent propane (C₃H₈) and 70 percent butane (C₄H₁₀) on a volume basis is burned in air such that the air–fuel ratio is 20 kg air/kg fuel and combustion is complete. The kmol of O₂ in the products per kmol of fuel is (use the exact molar masses of A-1/A-27: M_air = 28.97; C₃H₈ 44.097; C₄H₁₀ 58.123) [Added: the molar-mass hint, not in the original statement]:
pool.e: Fuel: C = 0.3×3 + 0.7×4 = 3.7; H = 0.3×8 + 0.7×10 = 9.4; M = 53.916 kg/kmol ⇒ AF_th = 15.474 and λ = 20/AF_th = 1.2925. Air = 20 × 53.916/28.97 = 37.22 kmol ⇒ O₂ in = 7.820; N₂ = 29.40 (printed 29.41); H₂O = 4.7 (printed 4.7); O₂ out = O₂ in − (C + H/4) = 7.820 − 6.050 = 1.770 (printed 1.77). With rounded masses (29; 12; 1) the result is 1.74: it is sensitive to the rounding convention because it is a difference of two close numbers. 2.77 kmol/kmol adds one kmol by mistake. 7.82 kmol/kmol is the total O₂ supplied (7.82), not yet minus the O₂ consumed. 0.00 kmol/kmol assumes theoretical combustion leaves no O₂.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–104 (part c)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–53 (part b). Acetylene (C₂H₂) is burned completely with 20 percent excess air in a steady-flow combustion chamber. The fuel and air enter at 25 °C and the products leave at 1500 K. The heat transferred out of the chamber per kmol of C₂H₂ (A-26, A-18…A-23) is:
pool.e: Reactants: C₂H₂ + 3 (O₂ + 3.76 N₂); products: 2 CO₂ + 1 H₂O + 0.5 O₂ + 11.28 N₂ (AF = 15.9 kg/kg, part a). Q_out = H_react − H_prod, H_react = +226,730 (h̄_f°(C₂H₂)); H_prod = Σ N(h̄_f° + h̄(1500 K) − h̄(298 K)) with the differences: CO₂ 61,714; H₂O 48,095; O₂ 40,610; N₂ 38,404 kJ/kmol ⇒ H_prod = −403,835; Q_out = 630,565 kJ/kmol. The same route was tested on Problems 15–55, 15–56, 15–60, 15–67, 15–70 (printed answers reproduced). 1,255,590 kJ/kmol counts only −Σ N h̄_f° (combustion at 25 °C) and drops the sensible enthalpy of the products. 722,670 kJ/kmol uses liquid H₂O at 1500 K (wrong phase). 707,373 kJ/kmol adds the enthalpy of two extra kmol of N₂ to the products.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–53 (part b)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–55 (part b). Benzene gas (C₆H₆) at 25 °C is burned in a steady-flow process with 95 percent theoretical air entering at 25 °C. All the hydrogen burns to H₂O but part of the carbon burns to CO; the products leave at 1000 K. The heat transferred out of the chamber (kJ/kmol C₆H₆) is:
pool.e: C₆H₆ + 7.125 (O₂ + 3.76 N₂) → 5.25 CO₂ + 0.75 CO + 3 H₂O + 26.79 N₂ (O: 14.25 = 2x + y + 3 and x + y = 6). Q_out = 82,930 − [5.25(−393,520 + 33,405) + 0.75(−110,530 + 21,686) + 3(−241,820 + 25,978) + 26.79 × 21,460] = 2,112,779 kJ/kmol (printed answer 2,112,800; difference 0.0010 %). CO mole fraction = 0.75/35.79 = 2.1 % (part a, printed 2.1 %). 2,957,268 kJ/kmol drops the sensible enthalpy of the products (only −Σ N h̄_f°). 2,285,974 kJ/kmol assumes complete combustion to CO₂ with 100 % air. 2,325,022 kJ/kmol counts the 0.75 kmol of CO as CO₂ (ignores the formation-enthalpy difference).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–55 (part b)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–56. Diesel fuel (C₁₂H₂₆) at 25 °C is burned in a steady-flow combustion chamber with 20 percent excess air that also enters at 25 °C. The products leave at 500 K. Assuming complete combustion, the fuel mass flow rate needed to supply heat at 2000 kJ/s is:
pool.e: C₁₂H₂₆ + 18.5 (O₂ + 3.76 N₂) is the stoichiometric equation: a_th = 12 + 6.5 = 18.5; 20 % excess → 22.2 O₂ → products 12 CO₂ + 13 H₂O + 3.7 O₂ + 83.5 N₂. Q_out = 6,869,098 kJ/kmol (h̄_f° of C₁₂H₂₆(g) = −291,010 from A-26 and h̄ − h̄_298 from A-18…A-23 at 500 K). ṁ = 2000 kJ/s × 170 kg/kmol / 6,869,098 kJ/kmol = 0.04950 kg/s = 49.5 g/s (printed answer 49.5). 44.9 g/s drops the sensible enthalpy of the products (uses |h̄_C| only). 0.8 g/s reads 2000 kJ/min instead of 2000 kJ/s. 58.0 g/s reads 500 K as 500 °C (773 K).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–56

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–60. Ethane gas (C₂H₆) at 25 °C is burned at a rate of 5 kg/h in a steady-flow combustion chamber with the stoichiometric amount of air preheated to 500 K. The gas analysis shows that all the hydrogen burns to H₂O but only 95 percent of the carbon burns to CO₂ and 5 percent forms CO. The products leave at 800 K. The rate of heat transfer from the chamber (kJ/h) is:
pool.e: C₂H₆ + 3.5 (O₂ + 3.76 N₂) → 1.9 CO₂ + 0.1 CO + 3 H₂O + 0.05 O₂ + 13.16 N₂ (O₂ left: 3.5 − 1.9 − 0.05 − 1.5 = 0.05). Q_out = H_react − H_prod = 1,201,005 kJ/kmol; mole rate = 5/30 = 0.1667 kmol/h ⇒ 200,167 kJ/h (printed answer 200,170; with M = 30.07 it is 199,701). 183,649 kJ/h takes the air as entering at 25 °C (drops the preheating enthalpy at 500 K). 1,201,005 kJ/h is kJ per kmol of fuel, not multiplied by 5/30 kmol/h. 220,184 kJ/h adds 10 % (bad rounding).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–60

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–67. Liquid ethyl alcohol (C₂H₅OH(ℓ)) at 25 °C is burned in a steady-flow chamber with 40 percent excess air that also enters at 25 °C. The products leave at 600 K, complete combustion. The volume flow rate of liquid ethanol required to supply heat at 2000 kJ/s (density 790 kg/m³, M = 46 kg/kmol) is:
pool.e: C₂H₅OH + 3 O₂ → 2 CO₂ + 3 H₂O; 40 % excess → 4.2 O₂, 15.79 N₂, products 2 CO₂ + 3 H₂O + 1.2 O₂ + 15.79 N₂. Q_out = 1,025,934 kJ/kmol (h̄_f° of liquid ethanol, A-26). ṁ = 2000/1,025,934 × 46 = 0.090 kg/s ⇒ V̇ = 0.11351 L/s = 6.81 L/min (printed answer 6.81). 6.54 L/min uses h̄_f° of ethanol VAPOR (−235,310) instead of liquid (−277,690). 0.11 L/min forgets to convert s to min (gives L/s). 5.38 L/min multiplies by the density instead of dividing (gives kg/min).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–67

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–70. Hydrogen (H₂) at 7 °C is burned with 20 percent excess air that is also at 7 °C during an adiabatic steady-flow combustion process. Assuming complete combustion, the exit temperature of the products (A-18…A-23) is about:
pool.e: H₂ + 0.6 (O₂ + 3.76 N₂) needs a_th = 0.5; 20 % excess → 0.6 O₂, 2.256 N₂; products H₂O + 0.1 O₂ + 2.256 N₂. Adiabatic condition: Σ N_p(h̄_f° + h̄(T) − h̄_298) = Σ N_r(h̄_f° + h̄(280 K) − h̄_298), right side = −2,033 kJ/kmol. Try T = 2250 K: left side −2,229; T = 2300 K: 4,706 ⇒ interpolation T = 2,251.4 K (printed answer 2251.4 K). 2,511 K drops the 20 % excess air (λ = 1): too little inert gas to absorb the heat. 1,534 K reads 20 % excess as 120 % excess (λ = 2.2). 2,416 K adds 150 K (misapplied reactant sensible enthalpy).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–70

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–73. Acetylene gas (C₂H₂) at 25 °C is burned in a steady-flow process with 30 percent excess air at 27 °C. Heat is lost to the surroundings at 75,000 kJ per kmol of C₂H₂. Assuming complete combustion, the exit temperature of the products (A-18…A-23) is about:
pool.e: C₂H₂ + 3.25 (O₂ + 3.76 N₂) → 2 CO₂ + H₂O + 0.75 O₂ + 12.22 N₂. H_react = 226,730 + the enthalpy of the 3.25 × 4.76 kmol of air at 300 K: 227,565 kJ/kmol; H_prod(T) = H_react − 75,000 = 152,565 ⇒ interpolation in A-18…A-23: T = 2,303 K (printed answer 2301 K; gap 2 K ≈ 0.09 % from linear interpolation/rounding). 2,418 K ignores the 75,000 kJ/kmol heat loss (treats it as adiabatic). 2,767 K drops the 30 % excess air. 2,533 K adds the 75,000 instead of subtracting (wrong sign of the loss).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–73

pool.q: Cengel Example 15–8 (part a, added from §15-5). Liquid octane (C₈H₁₈) at 25 °C and 1 atm is burned with the theoretical amount of air entering at the same state in an adiabatic steady-flow gas-turbine combustor, complete combustion. The product temperature (A-18…A-23, trial and interpolation) is about:
pool.e: C₈H₁₈ + 12.5 (O₂ + 3.76 N₂) → 8 CO₂ + 9 H₂O + 47 N₂; H_prod = H_react = h̄_f°(C₈H₁₈ ℓ) = −249,950 kJ/kmol ⇒ Σ N_p(h̄_f° + h̄ − h̄_298) = −249,950 ⇒ 8 h̄_CO₂ + 9 h̄_H₂O + 47 h̄_N₂ = 5,646,081 kJ (book). Trial 2400 K: 5,660,828 (book 5,660,828, higher), 2350 K is lower ⇒ interpolation T = 2,395 K (book 2395 K). This adiabatic flame temperature exceeds the material limits of a turbine, so real combustors use a lot of excess air: 400 % gives 962 K (book 962 K). 962 K is the result with 400 percent theoretical air (part b of the book). 1,827 K has 50 percent excess air added. 2,682 K 12 % too high (small constant c̄_p used).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Example 15–8 (part a)

pool.q: Cengel Example 15–10 (part a, added from §15-5). Methane (CH₄) gas at 25 °C and 1 atm is burned completely with 50 percent excess air entering at 25 °C and 1 atm in an adiabatic steady-flow combustion chamber. The product temperature (A-18…A-23) is about:
pool.e: CH₄ + 3 (O₂ + 3.76 N₂) → CO₂ + 2 H₂O + O₂ + 11.28 N₂; Σ N_p(h̄_f° + h̄ − h̄_298) = h̄_f°(CH₄) = −74,850 ⇒ h̄_CO₂ + 2 h̄_H₂O + h̄_O₂ + 11.28 h̄_N₂ = 937,950 kJ (book) ⇒ trial and interpolation in A-18…A-23: T = 1,789 K (book 1789 K). 2,328 K ignores the excess air (λ = 1). 1,280 K reads 50 % excess as 250 % theoretical. 2,189 K adds 400 K (reactant N₂ sensible enthalpy).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Example 15–10 (part a)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–118 (FE). A fuel is burned with 90 percent theoretical air. This is equivalent to:
pool.e: Deficiency = 100 % − 90 % = 10 % (slide p.24: 90 percent theoretical = 10 percent deficiency). EXCESS air exists only above 100 percent theoretical (150 percent theoretical = 50 percent excess); 100 percent theoretical is the stoichiometric amount.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–118 (FE exam)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–119 (FE). Propane (C₃H₈) is burned with 150 percent theoretical air. The air–fuel mass ratio of this process is:
pool.e: C₃H₈ + 5 O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 4 H₂O: a_th = 5; 150 % → 7.5 O₂ → 7.5 × 4.76 = 35.7 kmol of air; AF = 35.7 × 29/44 = 23.53 (with M_air = 28.97 and 44.097: 23.46): the nearest option is 23.4. 15.7 is the theoretical AF (1.0 × 5 × 4.76 × 29/44); 10.5 is half of it.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–119 (FE exam)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–120 (FE). One kmol of methane (CH₄) is burned with an unknown amount of air. If the combustion is complete and there are 2 kmol of free O₂ in the products, the air–fuel mass ratio is:
pool.e: O₂ in = a_th + 2 = 2 + 2 = 4 kmol (a_th = 2); air = 4 × 4.76 = 19.04 kmol; AF = 19.04 × 29/16 = 34.51 (with M_air = 28.97 and 16.043: 34.38): the nearest option is 34.3. 17.2 is the theoretical AF (2 kmol O₂ instead of 4).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–120 (FE exam)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–123 (FE). Methane (CH₄) is burned completely with 80 percent excess air in a steady-flow combustion process. Reactants and products are both at 25 °C and 1 atm and the water in the products is liquid. The heat transfer from the combustion chamber per unit mass of methane is:
pool.e: |h̄_C| = 890,330 kJ/kmol (liquid water, 25 °C; the excess air enters and leaves at the same standard state so it has no effect) ⇒ 890,330/16.043 = 55,496 kJ/kg = 55.5 MJ/kg ≈ 56 MJ/kg. 890 is MJ per kmol (not divided by M); 802 is the LHV per kmol; 50 MJ/kg is the LHV per kg (50,050 kJ/kg).
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–123 (FE exam)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–124 (FE). The higher heating value of a hydrocarbon fuel CₙHₘ with m = 8 is given to be 1560 MJ/kmol of fuel. Then its lower heating value is:
pool.e: m = 8 means 8 H atoms ⇒ 4 kmol H₂O per kmol of fuel; h_fg of water at 25 °C = 44,000 kJ/kmol (2441.7 kJ/kg × 18.015); LHV = HHV − 4 × 44,000 = 1560 − 176 = 1,384 MJ/kmol. 1208 subtracts 8 H₂O; 1514 and 1551 subtract about 1 and 0.2 kmol of H₂O.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–124 (FE exam)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–125 (FE). Acetylene gas (C₂H₂) is burned completely during a steady-flow combustion process. The fuel and the air enter at 25 °C and the products leave at 1500 K. If the enthalpy of the products relative to the standard reference state is −404 MJ/kmol of fuel, the heat transfer from the chamber is:
pool.e: Q_out = H_react − H_prod; the reactants are at the standard state so H_react = h̄_f°(C₂H₂) = +226.73 MJ/kmol (A-26: 226,730 kJ/kmol); H_prod = −404 MJ/kmol ⇒ Q_out = 226.73 − (−404) = 630.7 MJ/kmol ≈ 631. 227 forgets H_prod; 404 forgets the positive formation enthalpy of C₂H₂; 177 and 751 have a wrong sign on one term.
pool.s: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–125 (FE exam)

pool.q: Cengel Ch.15 Problem 15–126 (FE). Benzene gas (C₆H₆) is burned with 90 percent theoretical air during a steady-flow combustion process. The mole fraction of the CO in the products is:

N₂ = 25.38; total products = 4.5 + 1.5 + 3 + 25.38 = 34.38 kmol ⇒ y_CO = 1.5/34.38 = 4.36 % ≈ 4.4 %. The assumption "H burns completely" follows slide p.20 (oxygen has a greater tendency to combine with hydrogen than with carbon).
