pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.7: why does the N₂ of the air, although inert, still affect the outcome of combustion strongly?
o: Because it raises the O₂ concentration in the flame zone.
Because it reacts with the fuel to make large amounts of NO, which raises the heating value.
Because it enters the chamber in large quantity at low temperature and leaves at a much higher temperature, absorbing a large share of the chemical energy released.
Because it changes the stoichiometric coefficient of carbon.
pool.e: Slide p.7: N₂ enters in large quantity at low temperature and leaves at a much higher one, so it absorbs a large share of the chemical energy released (the flame is cooler with N₂ present). Only a very small amount forms nitric oxides; it neither raises the heating value nor changes the stoichiometric coefficients.
pool.s: Added – from slide Ch.4 p.7: N₂ absorbs energy

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.8: why is it important to predict the dew-point temperature of the combustion products?
o: Because the condensed droplets often combine with SO₂ in the combustion gases to form highly corrosive sulfuric acid.
Because below the dew point nitrogen starts to react with oxygen.
Because the dew point determines the moles of theoretical air.
Because condensed water raises the flame temperature.
pool.e: Slide p.8: below the dew point water vapor condenses and the droplets combine with any SO₂ to form highly corrosive sulfuric acid, so the stack and heat exchangers must be kept above it. Condensation does not raise the flame temperature and has nothing to do with N₂ or a_th.
pool.s: Added – from slide Ch.4 p.8: dew point and corrosion

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.10 gives the minimum ignition temperatures in air: gasoline 260 °C, carbon 400 °C, hydrogen 580 °C, CO 610 °C, methane 630 °C. Which substance needs the HIGHEST minimum ignition temperature?
pool.e: By slide p.10 methane has the highest minimum ignition temperature (630 °C), then CO (610), hydrogen (580), carbon (400) and gasoline the lowest (260). The fuel must be brought above this temperature to burn; contact with oxygen alone is not enough.
pool.s: Added – from slide Ch.4 p.10: ignition temperatures

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.19: which of the following is NOT among the causes of incomplete combustion named on the slide?
o: Too much N₂ in the air supplied.
Insufficient mixing during the short time the fuel and the oxygen are in contact.
pool.e: Slide p.19 lists: insufficient oxygen; more oxygen than needed (but insufficient mixing); insufficient mixing in the short contact time; dissociation (especially at high temperature). Extra N₂ is not a cause of incomplete combustion (it only lowers the temperature). Note: the real cause when oxygen is in excess is insufficient mixing (Cengel §15-2).
pool.s: Added – from slide Ch.4 p.19: causes of incomplete combustion

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.23–24: the stoichiometric amount of air is 100 percent theoretical air. 150 percent and 90 percent theoretical air correspond to:
pool.e: Percent excess = percent theoretical − 100 %: 150 % theoretical = 50 % excess; percent deficiency = 100 % − percent theoretical: 90 % theoretical = 10 % deficiency (p.23–24). 200 % excess = 300 % theoretical.

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.24: the equivalence ratio φ is the ratio of the actual fuel–air ratio to the stoichiometric fuel–air ratio. A mixture burned with 125 percent theoretical air has φ equal to:
pool.e: φ = (F/A)act/(F/A)st = (A/F)st/(A/F)act = 1/1.25 = 0.80 < 1: a lean mixture (air in excess). φ > 1 is rich (air deficiency). 1.25 is the inverse (φ confused with the percent theoretical air).
pool.s: Added – from slide Ch.4 p.24: equivalence ratio

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.26: on which basis does the Orsat gas analyzer report its result, and why?
o: Dry basis: the sample is collected over water and stays saturated with vapor, so the water vapor is not counted in the result; the H₂O formed is found from the balanced equation.
Wet basis: the sample keeps its water vapor at the combustion chamber temperature.
Dry basis: because the device first absorbs the H₂O and only then measures the CO₂.
Mass basis: the device weighs each gas.
pool.e: Orsat reports volume fractions on a dry basis (p.26; Cengel: the sample is collected over water and stays saturated so the vapor pressure is constant and ignored). Volume fraction equals mole fraction for ideal gases; the H₂O formed is found from the balance (coefficient b of Example 15–4). It does not measure mass.
pool.s: Added – from slide Ch.4 p.26: Orsat analyzer

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.31: the dew-point temperature of the combustion products (ideal gases) equals:

the temperature at which N₂ condenses
the saturation temperature of water at the partial pressure of the water vapor, P_v = (N_v/N_prod) P_prod
pool.e: Dew point = T_sat(P_v) with P_v = y_v P_prod = (N_v/N_prod) P_prod (p.31–32). Using the total pressure gives about 100 °C at 100 kPa, which is wrong.
pool.s: Added – from slide Ch.4 p.31–32: definition of dew point

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.49: which of the following has a NON-zero enthalpy of formation h̄_f° at the standard state (Table A-26)?

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.51–52: the higher heating value HHV and the lower heating value LHV differ in that:
o: HHV is taken at a higher pressure, LHV at a lower one
HHV is for liquid H₂O in the products, LHV for vapor; HHV = LHV + m·h_fg
HHV is for H₂O vapor, LHV for liquid
HHV also includes the nuclear energy of the fuel
pool.e: Heating value = |h_C|; with liquid H₂O in the products it is the HHV, with vapor the LHV; HHV = LHV + (m h_fg)_H₂O, with m the mass of H₂O in the products per kg of fuel (p.51–52). For fuels without hydrogen (C, CO) the two are equal.
pool.s: Added – from slide Ch.4 p.51–52: HHV and LHV

pool.q: Slide Ch.4 p.3: unlike a non-reacting system, a reacting system also has to include in its energy balance:
o: the kinetic energy of the combustor casing
the chemical internal energy associated with the breaking and forming of bonds between atoms
only the latent internal energy of phase change
the nuclear energy of the atoms
pool.e: Slide p.3: a non-reacting system only needs sensible and latent internal energy; a reacting system also needs chemical internal energy (bond breaking and forming). Nuclear energy is not considered (p.42).
pool.s: Added – from slide Ch.4 p.3: chemical internal energy

pool.q: Cengel §15-1: for simplicity, gasoline is usually treated as which fuel, and diesel fuel as which?
o: Gasoline = methanol CH₃OH; diesel = propane C₃H₈
Gasoline = dodecane C₁₂H₂₆; diesel = octane C₈H₁₈
Gasoline = methane CH₄; diesel = octane C₈H₁₈
Gasoline = octane C₈H₁₈; diesel = dodecane C₁₂H₂₆
pool.e: Cengel §15-1: liquid fuels are mixtures of many hydrocarbons but are treated as one: gasoline ≈ octane C₈H₁₈, diesel ≈ dodecane C₁₂H₂₆ (natural gas ≈ methane CH₄). Slide p.4 only gives CₙHₘ and the distillation of crude oil into gasoline, kerosene, diesel and fuel oil.
